overview.text: Ludwig van Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55, is widely known as the “Eroica,” or “Heroic” Symphony. Beethoven worked on it mainly in 1803 and completed revisions by early 1804. Its four movements move from a forceful opening through a funeral march and lively scherzo to a finale built around a theme he had also used in his ballet The Creatures of Prometheus. The work’s scale and expressive range helped make it an influential response to ideas beyond music itself. Napoleon Bonaparte was connected with an early title, but the symphony’s documented dedication was to Prince Lobkowitz, and its intended heroic subject remains uncertain.

key_facts.text: The symphony is in E-flat major, Op. 55, and consists of four movements: an Allegro, a funeral march, a scherzo, and a finale.
Beethoven mainly worked on the piece in 1803, made final changes by early 1804, and it was first performed privately that spring at Prince Lobkowitz’s Vienna home.
Beethoven’s original dedication was to Prince Lobkowitz; an early title connected the work with Bonaparte, but the story of Beethoven tearing up the title page is not accurate.
The finale’s theme had appeared earlier in Beethoven’s ballet The Creatures of Prometheus, as well as in other works.
The symphony’s public premiere took place at Vienna’s Theater an der Wien on April 7, 1805.
